title: Propeller
object: Fixed-pitch, two-blade, forged-aluminium propeller of a four-seat light aircraft, Ø1905 mm, with its spinner and its bolting to the crankshaft flange: the blade from ahead, four blade sections and the hub in section
idea: A propeller is a rotating wing: each blade element meets a relative wind of forward speed and its own speed, and its lift, tipped forward, is the thrust
summary: At every station the blade meets a relative wind made of the forward speed plus the inflow it draws (axial) and its own speed ωr (tangential): the velocity triangle. The angle of attack is the blade angle less the helix angle, α = β − φ. Standing still at full throttle the triangles are flat, α is large and the root is stalled; climbing at 74 kt α is moderate; cruising at 110 kt it is small and the propeller is 85 % efficient; gliding with the throttle closed φ passes β − α₀ and the blades push back on the air: the propeller windmills. Thrust, power and efficiency against advance ratio J = V/nD come from blade-element momentum theory with a thin-aerofoil lift slope and a stall cap.
usedFor: Pilot training: why a fixed-pitch propeller's rpm rises with airspeed, why static rpm is a health check, what windmilling is
Aeronautical courses: blade-element momentum theory, velocity triangles, advance ratio, C_T, C_P and propeller efficiency
Maintenance: how a propeller is bolted to the flange (drive bushings carry the torque, bolts clamp, wired in pairs) and how the spinner is held
views: View from ahead 1:5, blade projected, stations B to E
Section A-A through the hub on both blades' pitch axes 1:2.5
Sections B-B, C-C, D-D, E-E at 30, 50, 75 and 90 % radius 1:2.5, with live velocity triangles
Diagram 1 C_T, C_P and efficiency against advance ratio
Diagram 2 blade angle and helix angle along the blade
Diagram 3 shaft speed and thrust over the tour
